title: Crab stitch edging
subtitle: How to work reverse double crochet for a twisted, rope-like border
excerpt: Crab stitch is double crochet worked backwards, from left to right. The twist in each stitch creates a corded edge that holds its shape and lies flat without rolling.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: Double crochet worked in the reverse direction (left to right for right-handers) so the stitch twists, creating a corded rope effect. Also called reverse double crochet.
The length of yarn attached to the ball or skein that you actively use to form stitches, as distinct from yarn tails or already-worked sections.

content.text: Crab stitch, also called reverse double crochet, is

: from left to right instead of right to left (for right-handed crocheters). The hook enters each stitch to the right rather than to the left, which twists the stitch and creates a firm corded edge. It is one of the most common finishing borders for blankets, garment hems, and amigurumi openings.
Complete any base round or row of edging that will underpin the crab stitch. Crab stitch is usually worked as the final round on top of a plain single crochet or double crochet border. Join the
at any point with a slip stitch. Do not chain up; the starting chain is not used in crab stitch.
With the hook in the loop and the work facing you, rotate the hook so it faces downward (the hook tip points toward the work).
Insert the hook into the stitch immediately to the RIGHT of the current position (backwards along the row).
Yarn over and draw up a loop. There are now two loops on the hook.
Yarn over and draw through both loops. One crab stitch complete.
Move one stitch to the right and repeat. Continue until you have worked all the way around.

Each stitch twists as it forms, producing a row that looks like a twisted rope or cord running along the edge. The border lies flat and does not curl. The texture is denser than a plain row of double crochet and the cord is firmer to the touch.

items.symptom: The edge pulls in and the fabric puckers
items.cause: Crab stitch is being worked too tightly compared to the base row.
items.fix: Go up one hook size for the crab stitch round only. The cord should sit snug but not compress the edge.

items.symptom: The stitches do not twist and look like normal double crochet
items.cause: The hook is entering from the left (forward direction) rather than the right (backward direction).
items.fix: After joining, consciously move the hook to the stitch on the right before inserting. The awkward angle of the backward insertion is what creates the twist.

items.symptom: The last stitch joins awkwardly to the first
items.cause: The number of stitches does not close evenly in reverse direction.
items.fix: Join with a slip stitch into the top of the first crab stitch rather than back into the join point. Weave in the tail on the wrong side.

content.text: Try crab stitch on the edge of a finished dishcloth before using it on a garment. The stiff cord shows up clearly on a flat square and gives you a chance to get the tension consistent without the pressure of a finished piece.
